body.text: More than two decades after the United States was declared measles-free, the country has officially lost its measles elimination status.
The decision, confirmed by the World Health Organization's Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) overnight, means measles is no longer controlled and is spreading locally in the US.
There have been more than 5,400 cases of measles reported in the United States this year, with six confirmed deaths and 590 hospitalisations.
The US along with Mexico and Bolivia join seven other nations including Canada and the UK that have been stripped of their measles-free status in the past year.
Director of PAHO Jarbos Barbosa said increases of measles numbers were a "serious worry".
"Measles is resurging globally amid a persistent gaps in vaccination coverage," Dr Barbosa said.

Peter Hotez, professor of paediatrics and molecular virology at the Baylor College of Medicine in Texas, said rising case numbers in the US were due to falling vaccination rates and medical "disinformation".
"Measles is back in a big way,"
"We've had horrific epidemics, beginning with the one in my state of Texas starting in 2025 … and now this current one in Pennsylvania, with significant numbers of deaths and hospitalisations."
Is Australia at risk of losing its own measles elimination status?
And what can people do to minimise their own risk of getting sick?
What is measles?
Measles is a very contagious viral illness that typically spreads by breathing in droplets sneezed or coughed into the air by an infected person.
These tiny infectious droplets can stay in the air for up to two hours after someone leaves the room.
Professor Hotez said measles could be "the most infectious virus agent we know".
Scientists use the basic reproduction number, known as R-naught or R0, to understand how infectious different diseases are.
Measles has a reproductive number of 12 to 18.

"That means if a single individual gets measles, they'll pass it on average to 12 to 18 unvaccinated individuals, and that's why it can spread like wildfire among unvaccinated populations," Professor Hotez said.
Symptoms include fever, cough, red eyes and a red or blotchy rash.
Measles can lead to serious illnesses including ear infections, pneumonia, inflammation of the brain and death.
Young kids, pregnant women and people with compromised immune systems are at higher risk of severe disease.
What does measles elimination status mean?
Measles elimination status, sometimes called measles-free status, is an honorary title given out by the World Health Organization.
It doesn't mean zero cases — imported cases from travellers are permitted — but that a country has no sustained or local transmission.
This status is revoked if the same measles strain spreads locally for a full year.
In January, six countries in the WHO's European region including the UK lost its measles elimination status, just months after Canada was stripped of the same title.
The US had been declared measles free for 26 years.
Dr Barbosa said losing a measles elimination status had broader implications than losing a public health designation.
"It means the virus has circulated for a prolonged period of time, putting families and communities at risk of a preventable illness, hospitalisation and death," he said.
University of Queensland infectious diseases physician and clinical microbiologist Paul Griffin said the decision came as "no surprise", considering how long the virus had been circulating in the US.
What's happening in the US?
The US is enduring its worst year for measles since 1991, according to the US Centers for Disease Control, with numbers growing significantly since the COVID-19 pandemic.

"You're starting to see clusters of counties with large numbers of measles cases, measles hospitalisations, now tragically, measles deaths, because of the spread of vaccination rate declines," Professor Hotez said.
Nearly one in five cases in the US are in kids under the age of five.
Most people infected are either unvaccinated or have an unknown vaccination status.
The largest US outbreak at the moment is in Pennsylvania, with more than 1,500 reported cases.
Amish communities have been directly affected due to low vaccination rates, leading to the deaths of six people.
Will Australia lose its measles-free status?
No, not right now.
Australia's measles elimination status was first verified in 2014 and is assessed annually.
Our most recent report, submitted in July 2026, included data up to the end of last year.
Based on this information, Australia met the criteria to keep its measles-free status.
But there has been a growing number of confirmed measles cases in Australia, mostly from travellers who unknowingly bring the infection into the country.
What should Australians do?
Measles is vaccine-preventable, so experts say it's important to make sure you and your family are fully vaccinated.
When fewer people are vaccinated, it's easier for the virus to spread, Professor Griffin said.

He said Australia needed 95 per cent of people to have received two doses of the combined measles, mumps and rubella vaccine, known as the MMR vaccine, to achieve herd immunity where virus spread is contained.
Children have one MMR vaccine at 12 months and a second at 18 months.
But Australia's vaccination rates have dropped since the pandemic.
Current vaccination coverage rates for one, two and five-year-olds in Australia are 92.8 per cent, 90.8 per cent and 93.3 per cent.
Australians born before 1966 are generally considered to be immune to measles. Anyone born after then, who doesn't have proof they've had two vaccines, can get a free catch-up vaccine.
Professor Griffin added that measles wasn't just a US or an Australian problem, but a global issue.
This meant it was important for anyone travelling overseas to check their vaccination status, and chat to their doctor if they were unsure.
